passage:
Asif, I have to tell someone. You know how everyone in the hostel comes to my room with their problems? Ravi even calls me 'Varun bhai, our therapist'. Ravi's break-up, Joseph's exam fear, my cousin calling every night about fights at home. I listen to all of it. I even did Joseph's assignment once so he'd calm down.
Last week I snapped at Ravi just for knocking. Then I felt awful. I'm tired all the time, and honestly a bit angry at all of them, which makes me feel like a bad person.
So I'm trying something. I still listen, but I set a time: after dinner, till ten. I stopped doing people's work for them. To my cousin I said, 'I care, and I think you should also talk to the counsellor at your college.'
It feels strange. But I slept eight hours last night.

qa.q: What did Varun once do for Joseph?
qa.a: Did Joseph's assignment so he'd calm down.

qa.q: Why does Varun feel like a bad person?
qa.a: Because Varun is tired and a bit angry at the people he helps, and that resentment feels wrong to him.

qa.q: What limits did Varun choose, and why do they help?
qa.a: Listening only after dinner till ten, not doing others' work, and pointing his cousin to the college counsellor; caring without rescuing leaves him rested.

qa.q: How might Ravi feel about Varun's new after-dinner time?
qa.a: Ravi may be surprised at first, but a rested Varun who doesn't snap is likely a better listener for him.

grounding: Shows a caring young adult worn out and resentful from absorbing everyone's problems, who starts caring with limits instead of rescuing.

passage:
I've roomed with Ira since first year, so I've watched it build. Ira is the one everyone calls: the girl down the corridor who failed a paper, the cousin in Guwahati, the homesick junior. Ira answers every time, even at 2 a.m., and once gave away her whole month's canteen money to a friend who was short.
Lately I've watched her go grey. She sleeps through her 9 a.m. class. When her phone buzzes, she flinches before she picks it up. Yesterday she muttered, 'Why is it always me?' and then looked guilty for saying it.
I don't know everything going on in her head. But this morning I saw her type, 'I can talk tomorrow at five, not tonight,' and put the phone face-down. She made tea and actually drank it hot.
Tenzin

qa.q: What did Ira give away to a friend who was short?
qa.a: Her whole month's canteen money.

qa.q: What does Ira flinching at her phone suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels drained and dreads the next request, even though she cares about the people calling.

qa.q: What choice did Ira make this morning, and why is it a healthy step?
qa.a: She texted that she could talk tomorrow at five, not tonight, and put the phone down, caring with a limit instead of rescuing at any hour.

qa.q: How might the people who call Ira be affected by her new limits?
qa.a: They may have to wait a little, but they'll still get Ira's care, from someone rested rather than resentful.

grounding: Shows, through a roommate's eyes, a caring young adult exhausted and resentful from absorbing others' problems, and a first step toward caring with limits.

passage: Nazia volunteered at the college peer-support desk on Mondays, but lately it felt like every day. Mohit messaged at midnight about his break-up; her roommate cried about marks; two juniors knocked on her door after dinner. She said yes to everyone. By the end of term she was sleeping through lectures and snapping at her own mother on the phone, then feeling guilty. When Mohit texted again at 1 a.m., she felt a flash of resentment that frightened her. At the next volunteer meeting, the counsellor who ran the desk said, "You can care without carrying. You don't have to solve everyone." Nazia put her phone on silent after eleven and started giving people the counsellor's hours instead of her own.

qa.q: When does Nazia volunteer at the desk?
qa.a: On Mondays.

qa.q: What did Nazia feel when Mohit texted at 1 a.m.?
qa.a: She felt a flash of resentment that frightened her, after weeks of exhaustion.

qa.q: What changes helped make Nazia's caring sustainable?
qa.a: Silencing her phone after eleven and pointing people to the counsellor's hours instead of her own.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel if Nazia doesn't reply at 1 a.m.?
qa.a: Mohit may feel a bit let down at first, but he can still reach the counsellor and Nazia the next day.

grounding: Shows a caring young adult who absorbs everyone's problems, grows exhausted and resentful, and learns to care with limits.

passage:
Pooja,
I want to say something carefully, because I care about you. For three months I've been your first call for everything: the fights at home, the exam panic, the flatmate drama. I've loved being there. But I've noticed I'm exhausted, and last week, when you called at 2 a.m., I felt resentful for the first time, and I hated that feeling. I think I've been trying to fix everything instead of just listening. So here's what I can do: I'll always listen when I can, I'll check on you every Sunday, and I'll help you find the college counsellor for the heavy stuff. What I can't do is be awake at 2 a.m. and still be a good friend. I hope that makes sense.
Divyansh

qa.q: When will Divyansh check on Pooja?
qa.a: Every Sunday.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel after the 2 a.m. call?
qa.a: Divyansh felt resentful for the first time, and hated feeling that way.

qa.q: What limits does Divyansh set, and why are they caring?
qa.a: Listening when possible, a Sunday check-in and help finding the counsellor, so the friendship can last without burning out.

qa.q: How might Pooja feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Pooja may feel a little hurt at first, but also cared for, since the letter is gentle and offers real support.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult exhausted by rescuing a friend, choosing to care with limits and point to professional help.

passage: Everyone calls me the hostel's listening ear. I'm Vijay, twenty-one, and for two years I said yes to every sad person who knocked: Dolma's family problems, my roommate's heartbreak, a junior who was homesick. I'd stay up till four. I thought that's what caring meant. Then one night, when Dolma called crying, I heard myself think, not again, and I felt like a terrible person. My sister said, "You're not a bad friend. You're an empty one." That hit. Now I say, "I can talk for twenty minutes," and I mean it. I point people to the counsellor when it's big. I sleep. And weirdly, I'm kinder now, because I'm not secretly angry.

qa.q: How long does Vijay now offer to talk?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel after thinking "not again"?
qa.a: Vijay felt like a terrible person, guilty for the resentment.

qa.q: What changed that made Vijay's caring healthier?
qa.a: Setting a time limit, pointing people to the counsellor for big things and getting sleep.

qa.q: How might Dolma experience the new twenty-minute limit?
qa.a: Dolma may notice Vijay is warmer and more present, even if the calls are shorter.

grounding: Shows a young adult worn out and secretly resentful from absorbing others' problems, who learns to care with limits.

passage:
First week of term. Vikas's hostel door was always open. He fixed Ramesh's laptop, lent notes to three people and stayed up till two listening to Usha cry about her breakup, then wrote half her lab report so she'd have one less worry.
Three weeks later. Vikas fell asleep in his own lab exam. When Usha texted "can u talk?? 😢" that night, he stared at the screen feeling tired and oddly angry, and didn't reply.
Next Saturday. He called Usha in daylight. "I care about you. I can listen for a bit, but I can't do your reports, and I think the hostel counsellor could help with the heavy stuff." She was quiet, then said, "Fair." They talked for twenty minutes. That night Vikas slept eight hours.

qa.q: What happened to Vikas three weeks later?
qa.a: He fell asleep in his own lab exam.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel when Usha texted that night?
qa.a: He felt exhausted and resentful, staring at the screen feeling tired and oddly angry, and he didn't reply.

qa.q: Which change made Vikas's helping sustainable?
qa.a: He kept caring and listening but stopped rescuing by doing her work, and pointed her to the hostel counsellor for the heavy problems.

qa.q: How might Usha feel when Vikas sets his limit?
qa.a: She might feel a little stung at first, then respected and supported, since he still listens and shows her where more help is.

grounding: Vikas absorbs everyone's problems until he is exhausted and resentful, then learns to care with limits and separate compassion from rescuing.
